title: Parts of a Flowering Plant
cardDescription: Flower parts and the stems, leaves, and roots that support them.
description: Take a closer look at a flowering plant with a crossword about its blossoms, supporting parts, and new growth.
focus: This puzzle moves from familiar leaves and roots to some smaller parts of a flower. The clues describe where a part is or what it does. A few botanical names sit alongside everyday garden words, with crossing letters to help.
solvingTip: Notice whether a clue asks for a whole flower, one small part, or something supporting the plant. Location words such as tip and underground can help. Use the short everyday answers before tackling the longer botanical terms.

Main plant structure that supports leaves and flowers
Usually flat green plant part that captures sunlight

answerNotes.PETAL: Petals are often the most colorful parts of a flower, but not every flower has large or showy ones. The clue uses often rather than treating color as universal.
answerNotes.SEPAL: Sepals are the outer flower parts that commonly enclose the bud. They are often green and differ from the petals inside them.
answerNotes.POLLEN: Pollen is made in anthers and can be transferred to a flower's stigma during pollination. It is not a seed, which develops later after fertilization.
answerNotes.ANTHER: The anther produces pollen and is part of the stamen. The slender filament supports it, so the clue identifies the pollen-producing part.
answerNotes.STAMEN: A stamen includes a filament and an anther. It names the whole structure, whereas anther names one part of it.
answerNotes.NECTAR: Nectar is a sweet liquid that can feed visiting animals. Some visitors sip it while brushing against flower parts, which can move pollen.
answerNotes.ROOT: Roots commonly absorb water and dissolved minerals and help anchor a plant. The clue says usually underground because some roots are exposed above ground.
answerNotes.VEIN: Leaf veins contain tissues that transport materials through the leaf. The branching pattern is the visible feature used in the clue.
answerNotes.POD: A pod is a kind of seed case, such as the one around peas. Not every seed-bearing structure is called a pod.

title: At the Flower Shop
cardDescription: Flower arrangements, containers, and the supplies used to put them together.
description: Visit the flower shop through a crossword about bouquets, familiar arrangements, and the supplies used to gather and display cut flowers.
focus: The clues focus on arranging and presenting flowers. Some answers name a container or supply, while others describe the shape of an arrangement or an action used to prepare it. Everyday words can take a particular meaning at a florist's counter.
solvingTip: Ask whether the clue describes something holding flowers, tying them together, or shaping the arrangement. A ring-shaped display, a ribbon knot, and a plain group of flowers have different names. Short supply and action words can help with longer shop and arrangement words.

To fasten a gathered bouquet with string or ribbon

answerNotes.BOUQUET: A bouquet is an arranged group of cut flowers. The word can also describe an aroma, but the reference to a gift selects the flower meaning.
answerNotes.FLORIST: A florist sells or arranges flowers. The clue asks for the person rather than the container or the arrangement.
answerNotes.VASE: A vase holds and displays cut flowers. A plant pot commonly holds roots and growing material, which is a different purpose.
answerNotes.FOAM: Floral foam can support stems in an arrangement. The clue uses the material name, not a recommendation about how to handle or dispose of it.
answerNotes.BOW: Bow means a looped ribbon knot here and rhymes with go. The spelling also has meanings pronounced like cow, so the floral setting helps.
answerNotes.SPRAY: Spray has a floral meaning: a branching stem or an arrangement of flowers. The clue does not refer to a mist of liquid.
answerNotes.WREATH: A wreath is arranged in a ring. Its circular form distinguishes it from a long garland or a hand-held bouquet.
answerNotes.GARLAND: A garland is a long decorative strand. Its length and strand form distinguish it from a circular wreath.
answerNotes.POSY: A posy is a small bunch of flowers. The word describes the arrangement rather than one particular flower species.

title: Cottage Garden Colors
cardDescription: Garden flower names identified by their familiar shapes and features.
description: Picture a colorful cottage garden while solving clues about familiar flowers and the shapes that help identify them.
focus: This puzzle is a collection of garden flower names. Clues point to a recognizable shape, growth habit, or familiar feature. Colors and flowering times can vary among varieties and locations, so the wording avoids treating one appearance as universal.
solvingTip: Look for the shape or growth habit described in a clue, such as hanging tubes or upright flower spikes. Several names also have familiar meanings outside the garden. Use the whole description because many garden flowers share a color.
words: Garden flower often associated with romance and prickly stems
Flower commonly pictured with a yellow center and white rays
Flower known for delicate papery petals and a seed-filled capsule

answerNotes.ROSE: Roses commonly have prickles on their stems. Everyday speech often calls them thorns, but prickle is the more precise botanical term.
answerNotes.IRIS: Iris names both a flower and the colored ring in an eye. The shared spelling provides a direct second meaning to help identify the flower.
answerNotes.ASTER: Aster is linked to a word meaning star. The daisy-like shape gives another cue besides the name's origin.
answerNotes.HOLLYHOCK: Hollyhocks carry flowers along tall upright stalks. The tall habit and arrangement of flowers help distinguish them from low bedding plants.
answerNotes.COSMOS: Cosmos is a garden flower name and a word for the universe. That second meaning gives a clue independent of flower color.
answerNotes.PANSY: Many pansies have blotches that suggest a face. The clue describes that familiar appearance without claiming that every variety has identical markings.
answerNotes.PETUNIA: Petunia flowers have a flared funnel or trumpet form. Shape is more useful than one fixed color because petunias come in many colors.
answerNotes.DAHLIA: Dahlias have many flower forms and sizes. Small pompon and large dinner-plate forms are examples, not features shared by every dahlia.
answerNotes.STOCK: Stock is a flower name here. The shop-supply meaning is a separate everyday use of the same word.
answerNotes.SNAPDRAGON: Snapdragon gets its familiar name from the blossom's dragonlike shape and opening action. The clue uses that shape rather than a specific flower color.

title: Visitors Among the Blooms
cardDescription: Winged flower visitors and the words for moving between blossoms.
description: Watch the flower visitors through a crossword about familiar pollinators, the parts they use, and their movements among blossoms.
focus: This puzzle connects flowers with visiting animals. Some clues name an animal or a body part, while others describe movement. Not every flower visit transfers pollen, so visiting and pollinating are treated as related ideas rather than identical actions.
solvingTip: Notice whether a clue asks for a visitor, a body part, or a movement. Some answers name insects, while another names a bird. Short action words can give useful crossings for longer animal names.

Feeding organ a bee can extend to reach floral nectar

To move with light rapid wingbeats among blossoms
To stop at a flower while moving through a garden
To drink a small amount of nectar
To lightly cover a surface with fine particles such as pollen
To move pollen from one place to another
An open flower visited by a pollinating animal
Sweet liquid a hummingbird may drink from a flower
Material carried from anthers that can reach another flower's stigma
A flower's smell that may help attract a visitor
Visible hue that can help a flower attract pollinators
To come to rest on a flower after flying

answerNotes.BEE: Bees can carry pollen between flowers as they forage. A visit can contribute to pollination when pollen reaches an appropriate receptive flower part.
answerNotes.BUTTERFLY: Butterflies typically have club-tipped antennae. This familiar feature is useful in the clue, though flower visitors should not be identified by color alone.
answerNotes.MOTH: Many moths are active at night, but some fly by day. The word often keeps the clue from making an absolute claim.
answerNotes.BEETLE: Beetles have hardened front wings that cover their flight wings. Some visit and pollinate flowers, although not every beetle is a pollinator.
answerNotes.HUMMINGBIRD: Hummingbirds are birds rather than insects. Their hovering flight and visits to tubular flowers distinguish the animal in this clue.
answerNotes.ANTENNA: Antenna is singular; antennae is the usual plural for insect feelers. The clue asks for one feeler.
answerNotes.NECTAR: Nectar is a liquid food source for many flower visitors. It differs from pollen, which is the material involved in the transfer described elsewhere in the puzzle.
answerNotes.POLLEN: Pollination involves pollen reaching a receptive stigma. Simply visiting a blossom does not guarantee that this transfer occurs.
answerNotes.COLOR: Color is the American spelling used here. Different pollinators respond to different visual cues; the clue does not name one color as a universal favorite.

title: Colors and Shapes in Bloom
cardDescription: Color words, flower shapes, petal patterns, and scent.
description: Describe the garden in a crossword about flower colors, familiar bloom shapes, patterned petals, and scent.
focus: The clues focus on how flowers look or smell rather than asking for plant names. Some answers are color words; others describe a shape, a marking, or the arrangement of petals. Familiar comparisons help identify the intended description.
solvingTip: Check whether the clue asks for a color, a shape, a pattern, or a smell-related word. Look for line markings or decorative petal edges. Some shape clues use everyday objects as comparisons, while petal arrangement clues use their own descriptive terms.

Rich yellow color often associated with marigold blooms
Purple hue that shares its name with a small spring flower

Hanging flower shape resembling an instrument rung by a clapper
Rounded open flower shape resembling a small drinking vessel
Flower outline with points radiating like a familiar night-sky symbol
Elongated flower cluster with stalkless blooms attached along its axis
Group of flowers growing close together
Long and hollow in shape, like a narrow pipe
Having wavy or crinkled petal edges, like gathered fabric
Having finely flounced or fringelike petal edges
Describing a garden flower with a basic rather than multiplied petal arrangement
Describing a garden flower with extra petals compared with its basic form
Marked with lines of contrasting color on the petals
Marked with small dots of color on the petals
Having a noticeable pleasant floral smell
The smell given off by a flower

answerNotes.VIOLET: Violet can name a purple hue or a small flowering plant. This clue uses the color meaning while mentioning the shared flower name.
answerNotes.BELL: Bell names the shape here rather than a particular species. The hanging form resembles the body of a bell.
answerNotes.CUP: Cup describes a rounded open form. Many different flowers can have that shape, so the answer is a description rather than a plant name.
answerNotes.SPIKE: In botanical use, a spike is an elongated cluster with flowers attached directly along its central axis. The clue gives that arrangement rather than merely asking for something tall.
answerNotes.TUBULAR: Tubular means shaped like a tube. It describes the form of a flower rather than its color, scent, or growing season.
answerNotes.SINGLE: Single describes a flower's basic petal arrangement in horticultural use. It does not mean that the whole plant produces only one flower.
answerNotes.DOUBLE: Double flowers have additional petals compared with the basic form. The term does not promise exactly twice as many petals.
answerNotes.STRIPED: Striped refers to lines of contrasting color. Spotted describes dots instead, so the kind of marking distinguishes the words.
answerNotes.FRAGRANT: Fragrant is an adjective describing a noticeable pleasant smell. Scent is the noun for the smell itself.
